knowledge.title: Database performance: N+1 queries — latency grows with row count; MEASURE query count first, then batch reads (Prisma include / WHERE IN). SQLite 'database is locked' is a separate write-transaction problem
knowledge.solutionUnderTest:
1) MEASURE FIRST: enable query logging (Prisma: new PrismaClient({ log: ['query'] })) and COUNT queries per request at TWO row counts (e.g. 10 and 100). N+1 shows as the count growing with rows; the goal is a count CONSTANT w.r.t. row count. 2) Replace loop-accessed relations with one batched read: db.post.findMany({ include: { author: true } }). CAUTION: 'include = one JOIN' is NOT guaranteed — relation loading may compile to a JOIN or to a small number of batched queries depending on ORM version, provider and relation shape. The verifiable requirement is the CONSTANT QUERY COUNT measured in step 1, not a presumed SQL shape. 3) Key lists: db.user.findMany({ where: { id: { in: ids } } }) then group in memory. 4) GraphQL servers: DataLoader coalesces same-tick lookups. 5) VERIFY the fix: recount queries at both row counts — constant count with growing rows = fixed; anything else is not. 6) Over-fetching: shape with select. Nesting depth of ANY level is a COST signal to examine (query complexity, payload size); the response ladder in order of preference: shape with select -> split into separate queries -> push aggregation into the DB (groupBy / raw SQL) -> ONLY for a measured, reproducible hot path: denormalize, accepting an explicit consistency trade-off. There is NO depth threshold that by itself proves denormalization is required. 7) SQLite lock errors are NOT fixed by batching reads. Check for: concurrent writers, long-running or interactive write transactions, missing busy timeout. Candidate mitigations to verify on your stack: PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL; busy_timeout; keeping write transactions short.

VERIFICATION PLAN (PLANNED — NOT EXECUTED; no evidence exists for v2 claims yet): V1 doc-based (NOT yet inspected): SQLite official docs on the rollback-journal lock states (RESERVED / PENDING / EXCLUSIVE) and WAL-mode reader/writer concurrency — confirm the corrected locking explanation. V2 experimental (sqlite3 available on the user machine; run in a temp dir via mktemp -d so nothing is written into the workspace): open two sqlite3 sessions on one DB; BEGIN a write in one; attempt a write in the other — observe the lock error; then set journal_mode=WAL and observe the reader proceed during a pending write. V3 experimental (requires Node + Prisma — NOT on the user machine; candidate env: the Z.ai sandbox with its pinned Prisma version): seed a small schema, count queries for findMany + include at 10 vs 100 rows with log: ['query']; assert constant count for include and linear count for the loop pattern. V4 doc-based (NOT yet inspected): Prisma docs on query logging and SQLite concurrency for the INSTALLED major version. This record must not be promoted until V1-V3 have produced evidence.

conclusion.glmInterpretation: All 4 bridge cases passed against real executions on the user's machine (first round). Measured: V0 on real SQLite (user machine, Python 3.14.4, sqlite 3.46.1) the N+1 loop pattern executes exactly 501 queries at 500 parents while the single JOIN executes 1 query, with the loop 26.3x slower (15.9ms vs 0.6ms) — query count is the primary signal and it grows with row count exactly as the record claims. V2 the locking experiment reproduced all four documented behaviors: with a 0.25s busy timeout a second writer receives 'database is locked' while another writer holds an open write transaction; with a 3s busy timeout the same write succeeds after the holder commits; after PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL a reader proceeds during a pending write ('ok rows=3') while a second writer is STILL blocked ('database is locked') — writers serialize even in WAL; the default journal mode was 'delete' (rollback journal). V1 the live-fetched official SQLite documentation (lockingv3.html, wal.html, busy_timeout.html) contains the RESERVED and PENDING lock-state definitions verbatim, 'since there is only one WAL file, there can only be one writer at a time', 'readers do not block writers and a writer does not block readers', and the busy-handler sleep semantics — the record's corrected locking explanation matches the documentation. V4 the live-fetched Prisma v6 documentation (observability-and-logging/logging, queries/query-optimization-performance) documents the new PrismaClient({log:['query',...]}) configuration, event-based logging via $on, defines the n+1 problem ('one additional query per result'), and states the batching nuance that the dataloader 'does not currently batch findMany() queries'. SUPPLEMENTARY (Z.ai sandbox VM, Prisma 6.19.2 — labeled, not bridge-executed): the loop pattern ran 11 queries at 10 rows growing to 101 at 100 rows, while findMany({include:{children:true}}) ran a CONSTANT 2 queries whose captured SQL is two batched SELECTs (parents, then children WHERE parentId IN (?..)) — NOT a single JOIN. This directly verifies the record's corrected claim that 'include = one JOIN' is NOT guaranteed: on this ORM version and provider it compiles to two batched queries, and the verifiable requirement is the constant query count.

(3) The V4 doc quotes come from the live v6 docs; Prisma's behavior may change across major versions (the docs mention relationStrategy and dataloader evolution), which is precisely why the record mandates measuring query count rather than assuming SQL shape.
